n: The Canaanite king of Arad, in the Negev desert to the south, attacks Israel and takes captives. This is the same region where Israel had been defeated years earlier.

f.g: A Canaanite city in the Negev; archaeologists have excavated a site of that name east of Beersheba.
Hebrew Negev — the dry southern region of Canaan.

n: Israel vows to the Lord: if He gives them victory, they will completely devote these cities to Him, keeping none of the spoil for themselves.

f.g: Hebrew ḥaram — to devote wholly to God, usually by destruction, so no one profits from the war.

n: The Lord answers, and Israel wins. The place is named Hormah, meaning “destruction.” Notice the contrast: where they once lost by going without God (14:45), now they win by relying on Him.

f.g: hearkened = listened, heard

n: Because Edom refused passage, Israel must take a long, hot detour around its territory. The people grow deeply discouraged by the hard road.

f.g: compass = go around

f.w: the soul of the people was much discouraged
f.g: Literally “the soul of the people grew short” — they ran out of patience.

n: Again they complain against God and Moses, even calling the manna “light bread” — worthless food. They despise the very miracle that kept them alive.

f.g: Contemptible, worthless bread — their insulting name for manna.
loatheth = detests, is sick of

n: The Lord sends venomous snakes; many people die. “Fiery” may describe the burning pain of their bite.

f.g: Hebrew seraphim — “burning ones,” likely named for the burning effect of their venom.

n: This time the people admit their sin and ask Moses to pray for them. Moses, once again, intercedes for those who criticized him.

f.g: A rare, honest confession from the wilderness generation.

n: God does not simply remove the snakes. Instead He tells Moses to make a bronze serpent on a pole: anyone bitten who looks at it will live. Healing comes through faith-filled looking.
Moses makes the bronze serpent, and whoever looks lives. Jesus taught that this pointed to Him lifted on the cross; the Book of Mormon adds that many refused to look because it seemed too simple.

f.g: beheld = looked at, saw

n: Israel moves on and camps at Oboth. The trip toward Moab continues.
They next camp at Ije-abarim, east of Moab, toward the sunrise.

f.g: “Ruins of Abarim” — on the edge of Moab.
sunrising = east

n: Next they camp in the valley of Zared, a stream marking Moab’s southern border.

f.g: Also spelled Zered — a valley running into the southern Dead Sea.

n: They camp beyond the Arnon River, the border between Moab and the Amorite kingdom to the north.

f.g: A deep river gorge flowing west into the Dead Sea.

n: The writer quotes a lost ancient book, “the book of the wars of the LORD,” probably a collection of victory songs. The Bible sometimes cites sources it did not preserve.

f.w: book of the wars of the LORD
f.g: A lost record; compare the book of Jasher in Joshua 10:13.

n: The quotation describes the streams flowing toward Ar, a town on Moab’s border.

f.g: A Moabite city or region, mentioned again in Deuteronomy 2:9.

n: At Beer (meaning “well”), God promises water without anyone needing to complain first — a happy change.

f.g: Hebrew for “well.”

n: Israel sings a joyful song to the well. After so much murmuring about water, here is gratitude.

f.g: An ancient work song, perhaps sung while digging or drawing water.

n: The leaders dug the well with their staffs under Moses’ direction. Then the people traveled on to Mattanah, whose name means “gift.”

f.g: Probably Moses, or a leader with a ruler’s staff.
staves = staffs, rods

n: The journey continues through Nahaliel and Bamoth.

f.g: “High places” — perhaps the same as Bamoth-baal (22:41).

n: They reach the heights of Pisgah overlooking the wasteland. From a Pisgah peak Moses would later view the promised land before he died.

f.g: “Wasteland” or desert, perhaps the barren area northeast of the Dead Sea.

n: Israel sends messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, who ruled north of the Arnon.
The request is just like the one to Edom: let us pass on the main road, touching nothing.

f.g: The major trade route east of the Jordan.

n: Sihon refuses and attacks Israel at Jahaz.

f.g: suffer = allow

n: Israel defeats Sihon and takes his land between the Arnon and Jabbok rivers. They stop at Ammon’s border, which was strongly defended (and which God told them not to attack).

f.g: A river flowing west into the Jordan; Jacob wrestled there (Genesis 32:22).

n: Israel settles in the Amorite cities, including Heshbon, Sihon’s capital.

f.g: An important city east of the Jordan, near modern Hisban in Jordan.

n: Sihon had himself taken this land from an earlier king of Moab. So Israel did not take Moab’s land — they took land Sihon had already conquered.
Now the writer quotes a popular poem from the bards (“they that speak in proverbs”), likely an Amorite victory song once celebrating Sihon over Moab.

f.g: Poets or ballad-singers.

n: The poem pictures fire spreading from Heshbon, burning up Moab. Israel retells it with a twist: the conqueror has now been conquered.

f.g: Hilltop sites, often used for worship.

n: Moab is mourned as defeated, and their god Chemosh portrayed as powerless to save his people. The point: false gods cannot protect.

f.g: The national god of Moab (1 Kings 11:7).

n: The song ends describing ruin stretching from Heshbon to Dibon and Medeba — towns across the region.

f.g: A Moabite town where the famous Moabite Stone (Mesha inscription) was found.

n: Israel now lives in the former Amorite land.
Moses sends spies to Jaazer and takes its villages, driving out the Amorites.

f.g: A town north of Heshbon in good grazing land (Numbers 32:1).

n: Israel turns north toward Bashan, and Og, its king, marches out to fight them at Edrei.

f.g: A fertile high plateau east of the Sea of Galilee, famous for its cattle and oaks.

n: The Lord tells Moses not to fear Og: He has already given him into Israel’s hand. God’s word comes before the battle.
Israel defeats Og and possesses his land. These victories over Sihon and Og were remembered for generations as proof that God fights for His people.
